1:
The chapter opens a register, and Gill states its terms: these are the priests and Levites who came up out of Babylon with Zerubbabel the prince and Jeshua the high priest — the same man called Joshua elsewhere — with the priestly names running through this verse and the six that follow. Delitzsch treats the verse as the title of the first list and reads the subscription that closes it, which calls these the heads of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua; the brethren, he explains, are the Levites, as fellow-tribesmen and assistants of the priests.

What Delitzsch does with the list is to connect it to two others. Twenty-two heads are named, and the same names reappear further down as the names of priestly houses, paired there with the men who represented those houses a generation later — the small differences between the two forms he puts down to copying. Fifteen of the twenty-two have already appeared as heads who sealed the covenant to keep the law, which tells him something about how this chapter came together. Gill notices the same overlap from the other end, remarking that the names in the second verse stand among the sealers, and recording that one of them turns up later under a slightly altered form.

The Levitical names that follow bring two further identifications. Delitzsch finds four of them among the sealers as well, and suspects that one name absent from every other Levitical list in these books is miswritten for a similar one. The last he identifies with some confidence: Mattaniah is most likely the Asaphite named elsewhere as head of the first band of singers, since the text here says he was over the songs of praise.

Henry stands back and asks a different question — why the register is here at all. He grants that it is little more than a list of names, and that the reason for inserting it does not appear on the surface; his own answer is that it keeps these men in remembrance, so that later generations might know to whom, under God, they owed the revival and re-establishment of their religion. That, he says, is how we do our part toward the promise that the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance, and it is a debt still owed to faithful ministers, that those who have spoken to us the word of God should be remembered. He adds a second purpose: such a list may have been meant to stir up the sons who inherited these offices and preferments to imitate the courage and fidelity of the men who held them first. It is good to know what our godly predecessors were, Henry says, because that is how we learn what we ought to be.

One caution of Henry's guards the reader against a natural mistake. Jeremiah and Ezra stand near the head of the list, but he supposes neither is the prophet nor the scribe — the fame of the one belongs well before this time and that of the other some while after — though both of those men were priests, which is what makes the confusion easy.
6:
Two small observations open the section, both about how the list is put together. Ellicott hears something in the conjunction that begins one of the names: it marks off those who did not seal the covenant, and he finds the same device used again further down. On the summary that follows he is careful — these men were chief genealogically, not by the courses, since the courses are complete in none of the lists. Clarke gives the courses their history instead: twenty-four orders, subordinate to one another as David established them, and continuing, he says, until the Romans destroyed Jerusalem.

The Levites come next, and the office that catches the witnesses' attention is the direction of the thanksgiving. Gill notes only that these Levites lived in the same times; Clarke identifies the man set over the thanksgiving as chief of the singers; Wesley describes the duty rather than the rank — he was to see that the psalms of thanksgiving were sung in the temple continually, at the due time and in the due manner. Delitzsch takes up the pair named after them and reads their position as musical rather than military: they stood opposite their brethren at the posts of service, forming the answering choir. He rejects the sense of watch-posts because a later verse rules it out, while admitting that the absence of the doorkeepers from the list is remarkable, and he declines a conjectural emendation of a name found nowhere else.

Then the high-priestly succession is dropped into the middle of the Levitical lists, and here the witnesses divide over who wrote it. Gill follows the line down to Jaddua and reports the identification of that man with the Jaddus of Josephus, who is said to have gone out in his pontifical robes to meet Alexander returning from Tyre and Gaza, to have won many favours from him, and to have brought him into the temple and shown him the prophecy that concerned him. If that identification stands, Gill argues, the paragraph cannot be Nehemiah's, since he could hardly have lived so long; and Nehemiah's own history seems not to reach past the third of these high priests. His conclusion is that a later godly man inserted the fragment under divine direction, as insertions were made in the books of Moses and Joshua.

Delitzsch reads the same paragraph as doing a job rather than intruding. The genealogy is a connecting link between the lists on either side of it, put there to explain how those lists are dated, since each is fixed by the name of the high priest then in office. He extends the principle to the Levitical list further on, which a later verse assigns both to the days of Joiakim and to the days of Nehemiah and Ezra — so it cannot belong to Joiakim's time alone, because Nehemiah's arrival found Joiakim's successor already in the office.

The second register, of the houses in the next generation, is where the arithmetic stops matching. Gill counts twenty heads in the son's days against twenty-two in the father's, and accounts for the difference by two houses that left no descendants to represent them. Wesley describes the same succession from the human side: as the fathers had been priests under the first high priest, so their sons served in their fathers' places under the second, some of those fathers probably still living and many of them dead. Ellicott notes that one name has changed its form between the two lists and another has simply dropped out, and he does not pretend to explain it — other anomalies of the kind can be pointed to, he says, for which no account can now be given.
22:
A second list follows, and the high-priestly names in it carry a chronological problem the witnesses work at from several directions. Gill identifies Eliashib as the third high priest of the second temple. Clarke reaches the last name and tells the story attached to it: Jaddua is probably the priest who went out in his robes with his brethren to meet Alexander as he advanced on Jerusalem after taking Tyre and Gaza, and who so impressed the conqueror that he spared the city, bowed himself before the priest, worshipped at the temple, and granted the Jews many privileges.

The date depends on which Persian king is meant, and Clarke reports the dispute without resolving it: one authority holds it must be the Darius whom Alexander defeated, another that it is the earlier king of that name, in whose reign Jaddua was born and under whose successor he held office. Wesley takes the earlier king, and adds the solution that follows from it — the Jaddua named here may be the father of the man who met Alexander rather than the man himself. That removes at a stroke the difficulty about how late the chapter reaches.

On the record itself the witnesses are brief and useful. Gill notes that some refer the book of chronicles mentioned here to a particular passage; Clarke denies flatly that it can be the book now in the canon under that name, since no such list is found there. Gill also marks the structure, observing that the thread of Nehemiah's own narrative, broken by the two intervening verses, is picked up again with the Levites in the days of the third high priest, and Ellicott says the same in his own terms — the account resumes with a list of the temple's serving officers, many of the names being those already met with.

Delitzsch works on the Levitical names. Four of them turn up repeatedly as heads of Levitical orders, and comparing the lists obliges him to strike out as a gloss the word that makes one of them the son of another. Set opposite these four are their brethren, whose business was to praise and to give thanks by the commandment of David; and Delitzsch notices that the phrase describing their arrangement, ward over against ward, is used elsewhere of the gatekeepers and is here transferred to the standing of the choirs. He and Gill agree that the men named next were porters at the temple gates, and Delitzsch closes the section by marking the final verse as the subscription covering both lists — dated, as Gill points out, by a high priest whose own grandfather had held the office back in Babylon.
27:
The registers give way to an event, and Gill suggests the one explains the other: so many priests and Levites took part in the dedication of the wall that the roll of them had to be set down first. He widens what was dedicated — not the masonry alone but the whole city, its gates and its houses — and argues from the lesser to the greater, since if a new house was to be dedicated then much more a new city, and most of all the holy city with the temple standing in it. The service was made by prayer and songs of praise, and, Gill has no doubt, by sacrifice; it was kept as a festival, and he passes on the Jewish tradition that it was afterwards observed yearly on a fixed day of Elul. He explains the interval too: the wall itself had been finished earlier, but the gates were not yet hung and nothing was ready for a dedication until that later month.

Delitzsch sets the same event in the book's sequence. The measures for filling the city with inhabitants having been carried out, the restored circuit of wall was solemnly dedicated, and these three verses describe the preparations. Only some of the Levites lived in Jerusalem; the rest had to be fetched in from the places round about, which is why the text says they were sought out. He also finds the wording awkward where it speaks of keeping the dedication and joy, and would either read it as keeping the dedication with joy or, following the Greek and Latin, strike the conjunction out.

Henry hears the contrast between this chapter and the ones before it. The building of the wall was read with fear and trembling; the dedicating of it comes with joy and triumph, and those who sow in tears reap in this manner. He takes the ceremony to have two meanings. It was a solemn thanksgiving for the mercy of having the work finished, felt the more keenly for the difficulty and opposition it had met; and it devoted the city in a particular way to God, taking possession of it in his name. Every city and every house of ours, Henry adds, ought to have holiness to the Lord written upon it — but this city had been holy as no other ever was since God chose to put his name there, and now that it was refitted the builders and inhabitants dedicated it afresh, acknowledging that they held it as his tenants.

Where the singers came from occupies the rest of the passage, and here the witnesses do not quite agree. Gill takes them to be the Levitical singers and the sons trained up to the work. Delitzsch reads the region named as the Jordan valley rather than the neighbourhood of the city, narrowing it to the southern stretch near Jericho where the valley widens westward, and identifies a second group of villages with a site some thirteen miles to the south-west. Gill likewise places one of the named settlements in the open country of the plains of Jericho, and Clarke identifies it as the village raised where Israel encamped after crossing Jordan under Joshua. Ellicott, however, puts the singers chiefly in villages to the north of the city, drawing the comparison with the temple servants settled in Ophel. Delitzsch closes with the reason the text itself gives, that the singers had built themselves villages round about Jerusalem.
30:
The ceremony begins with washing rather than singing, and every witness stops on it. Gill takes the priests and Levites to have purified themselves by washing their bodies and their clothes, perhaps with the sprinkling of the water of purification. Clarke describes a wider discipline — washings, abstinence from wine, and forbearing other things lawful at any ordinary time. Ellicott states the principle underneath: before consecration to God there must be cleansing from defilement, and he notes how emphatically the text says that the ministers purified themselves before they purified anything else. Wesley turns the same observation into a charge: those who would be instrumental in sanctifying others must sanctify themselves, setting themselves apart with purity of mind and sincerity of intention.

Over the gates and the wall the two commentators who describe the method part company. Clarke makes it a matter of clearing rather than of rite: nothing was needed but to take the filth away from the gates and the rubbish from against the wall. Ellicott makes it a rite, the gates and the wall being purified by sprinkling, as the men themselves had been purified by offerings and ablutions. The difference is not trivial, since one reading makes the wall clean and the other makes it holy.

Then the procession. Gill observes what the scene presupposes, that the wall was broad enough to be walked along, and that the princes went in procession upon it; he adds that the princes of Benjamin must be taken in under the name of Judah. Delitzsch reaches the same conclusion by a different road, reading the princes of Judah as the princes of the whole community, since the name is used for the returned people at large. He describes the arrangement Nehemiah made: two great companies of men giving thanks, forming two processions that went along the wall in opposite directions and came to a halt facing one another at the house of God. The word rendered thanksgiving, he notes, carries the sense of acknowledgement and praise and then of thankofferings, which is how it comes to name a company of singers. Gill adds only that the second half of the princes followed with Hoshaiah at their head.
33:
The names in the second company raise two small questions of identity, and Gill and Ellicott answer them differently. Gill insists that the Ezra walking among these men is not Ezra the priest and scribe, who is assigned his own station further along, but a prince who happens to carry the same name. Ellicott suspects something simpler, that the name duplicates the Azariah standing immediately before it. On the next pair Gill is firm again: Judah and Benjamin here are individuals, not tribes, and he cites Jarchi for it. Ellicott finds the grouping itself curious — laymen placed centrally, flanked by clergy ahead and astern.

The trumpets belonged to the priests' sons, as Gill notes, and Delitzsch puts their number at seven on the evidence of a later verse. Behind them came whoever headed that division of the Levitical musicians, trailed by his kinsmen — eight by name, Delitzsch counts — bearing the instruments David had devised, while Ezra the scribe led the whole column. Gill glosses those kinsmen as relations of the young priest just mentioned. Between trumpeters, instrumentalists and a scribe, the middle of this column was an orchestra under escort.

With the roll of marchers finished, the route resumes. Delitzsch traces it from the wall by the dung gate on to the fountain gate, and then straight ahead and up by the stairs of the city of David, along the ascent of the wall, above the house of David, as far as the water gate on the east. He equates that flight with the descent from David's quarter on the eastern slope — and then admits that the description as a whole is not quite intelligible to us, which is a good deal more useful than a confident reconstruction would be. Gill supplies one bearing that helps: the fountain gate lay to the south of the dung gate, so this company was working its way round the southern shoulder of the city before turning up the eastern slope toward the temple. He notes too that the trumpets in this part of the procession were sounded by the priests themselves, which fixes who was making the noise as the line climbed.
38:
The second company went the other way round, and Gill gives its direction plainly: to the left, along the northern stretch of the wall. Delitzsch follows its course through the named landmarks — from beyond the tower of the furnaces to the broad wall, then above the gate of Ephraim, the old gate and the fish gate, past the tower of Hananeel and the tower of Meah as far as the sheep gate — until it came to a halt at the prison gate. Nehemiah himself walked behind this company with half the people, so that the two bodies between them carried the whole assembly round the circuit of the defences they had built.

Two of the landmarks draw comment. Gill explains the gate of Ephraim by the road it opened, leading toward the territory that tribe had once held. Ellicott notices what is not said about it: the gate is missing from the account of the repairs, having apparently survived in reasonable condition along with part of the broad wall — so the procession passed at that point over masonry older than the work being dedicated. The northern circuit Delitzsch traces is the one thick with towers, which is where the old defences had held.

Wesley attends to the halt rather than the route. The company stood still and waited, as their brethren were waiting on the other side, so that the two might go in together in due order and complete the solemnity as one body. The pause is the point: neither half of the procession finished on its own, and the waiting was what made the two into one act of worship rather than two. Gill describes the meeting: having gone round by opposite ways they came together in the temple — in its great court, he specifies, since no smaller space would have held them. Ellicott adds a distinction that keeps the sequence of the afternoon clear. They stood outside first and entered afterwards to present their offerings; but the main interest of the day, he judges, lay in worship carried on under the open sky rather than within the building. The dedication was of a wall, after all, and the wall was where it had been performed.
41:
A second roll of priests is given at the meeting point, and Ellicott makes a small but useful observation about it: like the priestly names listed earlier in the procession, these are the names of individuals, and they are not to be found in any of the registers that fill the first half of the chapter. The two kinds of list are doing different work — one recording houses and courses, the other recording the men who were actually present on the day.

Gill notes only that these priests stood there with the rest, and that the eight names following them seem all to be of priests who blew the trumpets, so that the company at the centre was a body of sound as much as of persons. Seven had carried trumpets in the procession itself; here another eight are named at the point where the two halves met, and the singers sang out loud under an overseer of their own.

Then the sacrifices, and the joy. Gill reads the great sacrifices as many sacrifices, following Ben Melech, and supposes them to have been of the larger cattle; since a good number would have been peace offerings, the people feasted upon them, which is what made the day a festival rather than only a service — the people eating before God rather than merely watching an offering made on their behalf. Ellicott holds the order of the verse to be the point: it is full of joy, but the abundant offering comes before the rejoicing does, and not the other way about.

Wesley fastens on the detail that the children rejoiced with the rest. Their hosannas were not despised, he says, but are set down here to their praise. He draws the general rule from it: all who share in public mercies ought to join in public thanksgivings, which makes the presence of the children in the record an argument rather than an ornament — they had been kept safe behind the wall like everyone else, and the joy that is heard far off is the joy of a whole city and not of its officers.
44:
The dedication over, the chapter turns to what the day left behind, and Gill fixes the timing exactly: the appointments were made on the selfsame day, while the people were still in the frame of mind the service had put them in. Men were chosen from among the priests to oversee the chambers set aside as treasuries, to keep safe what was brought in and to see that it went to the use it was meant for. Delitzsch sets the arrangement in a larger frame, crediting the joint labours of Nehemiah and Ezra with restoring the enactments of the law for the conduct and the upkeep of public worship.

Henry reads these verses as a test applied to the thanksgiving itself. When the solemnities of such a day leave impressions on ministers and people that make both more careful and more cheerful in their duty afterwards, then the day has been accepted of God and has turned to good account — and that, he judges, is what happened here. The ministers were more careful of their work than before, encouraged to diligence and watchfulness by the respect the people had just shown them. When the joy of the Lord engages us to our duty and enlarges us in it, the joy proves itself.

What the officers actually did is described in a phrase that the witnesses read two ways. Gill and Wesley take it straightforwardly of the singers and porters: the singers kept their courses and were not wanting at any service beyond the morning and evening offices, and the porters kept the gates so that nothing and no one ceremonially unclean should pass in — that charge, Wesley adds, being precisely what God had prescribed to them. Henry describes the same division of labour, the singers attending in due time to their office and the porters preserving the purity of the house by refusing admission to the unclean.

Ellicott would divide the sentence differently. On his reading the priests and Levites kept the ward of their God and the ward of purification, and the singers and porters kept theirs as well, so that the clause covers the whole ministry rather than two of its branches; to keep the ward, he explains, is to observe the appointed times and seasons of sacrifice and thanksgiving. Delitzsch arrives at the same construction by grammar, supplying the subject from the opening of the verse, and he makes two textual repairs in passing — a conjunction wanting before one royal name, which the Greek and Latin supply and without which the sentence is too harsh, and another standing superfluously in the next verse, which he puts down to a copyist.
46:
The last two verses reach backwards and then forwards. Gill explains the appeal to the old days as an appeal to office rather than to sentiment: there were chiefs of the singers set over the rest to instruct them and to see that the work was done properly, and he names the heads of the three musical houses alongside Asaph. Ellicott hears something else in the phrase of old — a mark of the deference these chapters consistently pay to ancient precedent, new arrangements being justified by pedigree rather than by usefulness. It is an odd argument to modern ears and a natural one to a restored community, whose whole claim rested on continuity with what had stood before the exile.

Then the maintenance of the ministry, which is where the chapter ends. Gill reads the verse as a tribute to two administrations: while Zerubbabel and Nehemiah governed, the people did their duty and the Levites were paid their dues punctually and at the proper season. Clarke fills in the mechanism. The singers and the porters were supported by the people at large, and each received his portion daily; the things set apart for sacred use were delivered by the people to the Levites, and by the Levites presented to the priests.

Clarke takes the last clause to refer chiefly to the tithes — the people bringing them to the Levites, and the Levites giving a tenth of what they received to the priests. He stops on the word the verse uses for that transaction. To sanctify a thing here means to dedicate it to the sacred uses for which it was designed, and Clarke notes that this is a very general sense of the word throughout Scripture, not a ceremony added to the handing over. Ellicott compresses the same chain into a phrase: the Levites stand midway between laity and priesthood, collecting a tenth and surrendering a tenth of what they collect. It is a quiet ending for a chapter that began with a procession on the walls: the singing stops, and what gets recorded is that the men who sang went on being fed. Gill's emphasis falls there as well — the dues were paid at the proper season, not merely paid — which is the difference between a settled ministry and an occasional one.
